and under freeze Quarto would key the cache on the source of this page alone,
so flipping delivery.active would have no effect. The page therefore runs R in
CI, which installs knitr, rmarkdown and yaml for the render and readr and
datawizard for the chunk below (.github/workflows/publish.yml); a package that
the chunk starts to use has to be added there too.

The page uses the custom layout of the opening pages of the AR4DS sites: every
section is a fenced div with a home- class (styled in style/home.css), and the
format cards, the tasks and all the text are ordinary Markdown below. The
claim, the replication and the reproduction come from the facts file of the
case (D:\ACADEMIC\TEACHING\2026_OR_NCL\_planning\housing\housing-facts.md); the
other numbers are read from the committed data files by the chunk below. -->

```{r}
#| label: numbers
#| include: false
# Numbers quoted on the page, read from the committed data files of the case;
# the ends of the curve carry a true minus sign.
h_curve <- readr::read_csv("cases/housing/data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
h_analysts <- readr::read_csv("cases/housing/data/analysts5.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
h_emails <- nrow(readr::read_csv("cases/housing/data/housing_audit.csv", show_col_types = FALSE))
coded <- readr::read_csv("cases/housing/data/audit_original.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(ProperName)) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(hispanic_name = startsWith(TreatmentGroup, "Hispanic"))
tab_8ptrz <- xtabs(~ hispanic_name + ProperName, data = coded)  # r-style: keep – chisq.test() takes a table

h_spec <- nrow(h_curve)
h_sig <- sum(h_curve$b_pp < 0 & h_curve$p < 0.05)
h_sig_txt <- if (h_sig == h_spec) "every one of them" else paste(h_sig, "of them")
h_for <- sum(h_analysts$task1 == "evidence for the claim")
h_for_txt <- c("None", "One", "Two", "Three", "Four", "Five")[h_for + 1]
h_ends <- sub("^-", "\u2212", formatC(range(h_curve$b_pp), format = "f", digits = 1))
chi_8ptrz <- formatC(h_analysts$statistic_recorded[h_analysts$id == "8PTRZ"], format = "f", digits = 3)
chi_plain <- formatC(unname(chisq.test(tab_8ptrz, correct = FALSE)$statistic), format = "f", digits = 2)
```

# The housing-audit case {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.home-lead}
This site teaches reproduction, robustness and replication in R on one published claim, together with the reanalyses that the claim received in a many-analyst study and the replication that tested it with new data. It is part of Applied Replication for Data Skills (AR4DS), which teaches the same exercise on four cases.
:::

::: {.home-cta}
[Formats](#formats) [Read the case study](cases/housing/index.qmd)
:::

## The case {.unnumbered}

::: {.home-intro}
A field experiment published in 2017 sent the same short email to about a thousand public housing authorities in the United States, each signed with one of six names meant to indicate a white, a Black or a Hispanic sender. One sentence of its abstract became the claim that the course works on.
:::

> "Hispanic housing applicants were ... less likely to be greeted by name than were ... white counterparts" [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect, abstract]

The case study tells the story in six parts: the original study and its design, SCORE and Multi100, the five reanalyses, their effect sizes on the scale of Multi100, the replication with new data, and the data that you will use. The case teaches proportions and the chi-square test, the linear probability model set against the logit, what conditioning on a reply does to an experiment, randomisation inference and statistical power, on one file of `r format(h_emails, big.mark = ",")` emails, released into the public domain (CC0) and shipped with the workspace.

::: {.home-cta}
[Read the case study](cases/housing/index.qmd)
:::

::::

:::: {.home-rs .home-reveal}

::: {.home-r}
### Reproduction {.unnumbered .unlisted}

SCORE never attempted one, although the data and code are public. The four statistics that Multi100 recorded for the analysts reproduce exactly from the public file.
:::

::: {.home-r}
### Robustness {.unnumbered .unlisted}

`r h_for_txt` of the five Multi100 analysts found evidence for the claim. The `r h_spec` specifications of the curve of the claim put the gap between `r h_ends[1]` and `r h_ends[2]` percentage points, `r h_sig_txt` significant at 5%.
:::

::: {.home-r}
### Replication {.unnumbered .unlisted}

A preregistered audit of 3,050 housing authorities, with new names, found no significant gap (z = 0.66, p = 0.51).
:::

## Formats {.unnumbered .home-reveal}

::: {.home-intro .home-reveal}
The facilitator of a course chooses its format, and the link that you receive for a course leads to it. Each format is an ordered route through the pages of this site, with a sidebar that lists its parts, a slides page, and links at the foot of every page to the part before and the part after.
:::

:::: {.home-grid}

::: {.home-track .home-reveal}
### [Short session](tracks/housing-short/index.qmd) {.unnumbered .unlisted}

[Two halves, in the browser lab]{.home-meta}

Two halves, with nothing to install and nothing to submit: the claim and the five reanalyses, the estimand statement, the reproduction of one reanalysis of your choice, a look at the menu of analyses and the curve of the claim, and the replication with new data.
:::

::: {.home-track .home-reveal}
### [One-day workshop](tracks/housing-one-day/index.qmd) {.unnumbered .unlisted}

[Four parts, mainly in the browser lab]{.home-meta}

The claim and the credibility of social science, the estimand and the causal graph, the reproduction of one reanalysis chosen by each participant, and the robustness exercise at the centre of the day: the specification menu, the class chart and its submissions, the curve of the claim, the replication with new data, and one analysis declared before it runs.
:::

::: {.home-track .home-reveal}
### [Extended course](tracks/housing-extended/index.qmd) {.unnumbered .unlisted}

[Three days, built around the workshop]{.home-meta}

A first day on open research and the tools, the same for every case, the workshop as the second day, and a third day on the methods of the case, which ends with a report of your own, written in Quarto and kept under Git.
:::

::: {.home-track .home-reveal}
### [Self-study](tracks/self-study/index.qmd) {.unnumbered .unlisted}

[Five stages at your own pace, in R]{.home-meta}

The case for a reader who works alone, in R on your own machine, with the modules of the [companion](companion/index.qmd) between the tasks of the exercise and a project of your own at the end.
:::

## The exercise {.unnumbered .home-reveal}

::: {.home-intro .home-reveal}
Every format works through the same five tasks, or a selection of them. The short session centres on the first three and sends nothing to the class chart, while the one-day workshop, the Extended course and the self-study route take all five. The decisions that the tasks ask for fall into three groups: the question that the analysis answers; measurement, how the variables are built; and the model, how it is fitted and its uncertainty judged.
:::

:::: {.home-reveal}

<details>
<summary><span class="home-n">Task 1</span>The setup check</summary>

Check that your tools work before the rest of the work depends on them: the setup check of the browser lab, or the check script of the workspace.

</details>

<details>
<summary><span class="home-n">Task 2</span>The data, the estimand and the graph</summary>

Meet the data of the case, write the estimand statement behind the claim, and finish the causal graph that goes with it. The graph shows why a comparison of greetings among the replies alone is no longer protected by the random assignment.

</details>

<details>
<summary><span class="home-n">Task 3</span>The reproduction</summary>

Choose one of the five analysts and reproduce the value that Multi100 recorded for that analyst, from the public file of the original authors (OAs). The four analysts who recorded a statistic reproduce exactly. One of them, 8PTRZ, recorded $\chi^2$ = `r chi_8ptrz` where the plain test gives `r chi_plain`, and finding out why is part of the task.

</details>

<details>
<summary><span class="home-n">Task 4</span>The menu</summary>

Work through the decisions that lie between the data and a result, try alternatives one change at a time, and send one exploration to the class chart. The [decision map](cases/housing/map.qmd) lays every decision out.

</details>

<details>
<summary><span class="home-n">Task 5</span>Declaration and report</summary>

Declare one specification in a short preregistration, run it, report it, and find where it sits among the `r h_spec` specifications of the [curve of the claim](cases/housing/multiverse.qmd).

</details>

::::

The [exercise overview](cases/housing/exercise.qmd) sets out the five tasks in full.

## The course {.unnumbered .home-reveal}

:::: {.home-reveal}

<details>
<summary>What the course teaches</summary>

The main aim of the course is to introduce technical skills for modern empirical data analysis: finding the data and code of a study in an online repository, working with code so that another person (or your future self) can reproduce your steps, fixing your analytical choices in a preregistration before you run the analysis, and writing a live report that combines code and text.

These skills are taught through an applied 'replication' exercise. Participants reproduce one of the reanalyses that made up the Multi100 project, whose results appeared in *Nature* [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]. This case takes the claim of a field experiment published in the *American Journal of Political Science* [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect] and tests the statistical robustness of a claim made by the original authors (OAs). You will:

1. **Reproduce a published analyst's result.** Choose one of the five Multi100 analysts of the case, run the analysis that they ran on the public file, and find the exact value that it produced.
2. **Find out why five analysts got five different answers.** When you run the same code, you get the same result; but there are different analysis options to choose from, and the five analysts each made different choices. Working through those options involves engaging with and choosing between various statistical methods.
3. **State an _estimand_ and draw a causal graph.** Often, variation in methods and therefore results is driven by having an imprecise understanding of the *quantity* that the study is trying to estimate. That quantity is the *estimand*. Causal graphs, or directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), are a useful way to set out the relationships between the variables in your dataset and to decide what to adjust for.
4. **Preregister one specification.** Pick one defensible analysis from a menu of choices. Before you run it, fill in the preregistration block of your report, which is a shortened version of a real preregistration template: the claim you are testing, one option for each decision on the menu, and a sentence grounded in your causal graph on why the specification answers the claim.
5. **Run it and submit the result.** Your result appears as a point on a live chart, against the curve of the claim and, in a taught session, beside everyone else in the class.
6. **Read a specification curve and a replication.** Work out what the `r h_spec` specifications of the curve of the claim, taken together, can and cannot establish, and what the replication with new data adds.

The exercise follows the design of Multi100 on a smaller scale, with many analysts testing the same claim, each stating their analytical choices, and results reported in a form that allows them to be compared.

</details>

<details id="the-one-day-course">
<summary>The one-day workshop</summary>

The one-day workshop runs in four parts, with breaks and a lunch between them, and when a delivery is scheduled, the callout near the top of this page gives its date. Part 1 sets out the claim and the credibility of social science, with the three Rs (reproducibility, robustness and replicability), and SCORE and Multi100 in brief. Part 2 takes the estimand and the causal graph, and Part 3 the reproduction of one reanalysis, chosen by each participant. Part 4 is the robustness exercise: the specification menu, the class chart and its submissions, the curve of the claim, the replication with new data, and one analysis declared before it runs.

The Extended course builds two more days around the workshop, a first day on open research and the tools and a third on the methods of the case and a report of your own. The short session runs as two halves in the browser lab and sends nothing to the class chart.

</details>

<details id="running-the-analyses">
<summary>Running the analyses</summary>

The exercise is done in R, either in the browser or on your own machine. The short session needs only a browser, and the one-day workshop is taught mainly in the browser lab, with the workspace as an option. The Extended course and the self-study route are taught in R on your own machine: install R and an IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.) once, then download the ready-made workspace, a single zip file holding the analysis code, the data and a report to fill in. There is nothing to configure, so you open the folder and start working, and the workspace is yours to keep afterwards. The data of the case are in the public domain and ship inside the workspace. The [setup page](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/setup.html) on the AR4DS site walks you through the installation in plain steps.

The [browser lab](cases/housing/lab.qmd) holds the same exercise on a version of R that runs inside a browser tab, with the data in the page and nothing installed. It is the place where the short session and the one-day workshop are taught, the place to try R and the data before you have installed anything, and the fallback if a machine fails on the day. Anyone can use it, whether or not they are taking the course.

</details>

<details>
<summary>The companion</summary>

The [companion](companion/index.qmd) holds the teaching material of the course on this case, in three groups: tools, data and sharing, and methods. Every module keeps its own page and stands on its own, so you can read one for the skill that it covers or take it in the place that a format gives it. A single day has room for the exercise and very little else, which is why the workshop points to the modules rather than working through them, while the Extended course teaches some of them as sessions and the self-study route sets each module beside the task that first needs it.

</details>

<details>
<summary>SCORE and Multi100</summary>

The claim comes from the work of SCORE, a programme that put claims from published social and behavioural research through reproduction, robustness checks and replication, and the exercise follows the design of Multi100, its study of robustness. The AR4DS site describes [the programme and the record of the four cases of the course](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/score-multi100.html), and its page on [the Multi100 article](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/multi100-article.html) explains how the results of the analysts were placed on one scale and compared.

</details>

## Getting started {.unnumbered .home-reveal}

::: {.home-intro .home-reveal}
The short session needs only a browser. The one-day workshop is taught in the browser lab, with the installation of R, an IDE and the workspace as part of its preparation, and the Extended course and the self-study route work in the workspace from the start.
:::

:::: {.home-steps .home-reveal}

::: {.home-step}
### R and an IDE {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Install R, Quarto and an IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.), following the steps for your operating system. [Install and check](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/setup.html)
:::

::: {.home-step}
### The workspace {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Download the workspace of the case as a zip file, open it in your IDE and run the check script. [The workspace](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/setup.html#the-workspace)
:::

::: {.home-step}
### The browser lab {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Try the exercise in the browser, without installing anything; it is also the fallback when a machine fails on the day. [Open the browser lab](cases/housing/lab.qmd)
:::

## Chris Moreh {.unnumbered}

::: {.home-role}
Lecturer in Sociology, Newcastle University
:::

<!-- The biography is quoted from chrismoreh.com (source: D:/GitHub/chrismoreh-source/index.qmd), as CM asked on 2026-10-25, and copied verbatim from the opening page of the EU-frames site. -->

A social scientist interested in the political sociology of migration, mobility, ethnicity and nationalism.

Hailing from Transylvania, trained in anthropology and sociology at [Eötvös Loránd University of Budapest](https://tatk.elte.hu/en/) and [Central European University](https://sociology.ceu.edu/), and with a PhD from [Northumbria University](https://www.northumbria.ac.uk/), I currently work as a Lecturer (Assistant Professor) in Sociology at [Newcastle University (UK)](https://www.ncl.ac.uk/gps/staff/profile/chrismoreh.html).

I approach social research as a comparative, interdisciplinary and multimethodological endeavour. My work has combined ethnographic observation, document analysis, survey methods and statistical modelling.

I'm enthusiastic about transparency and reproducibility in the social sciences, and my [pedagogical approach](https://www.ncl.ac.uk/mediav8/library/file-downloads/research-services/open-research/moreh.pdf) seeks to develop skills that facilitate open and credible research practices.

[chrismoreh.com](https://chrismoreh.com)
